title_ar: حكم الصلاة في مسجد أقيم في مكان غير مشرع
title_en: The Ruling on Praying in a Mosque Built on Land Not Lawfully Allocated
body_ar: بعض الأئمة في الجمعة الماضية يقول بأن الصلاة في هذا المسجد ليست صحيحة وذلك لأنه مكزور؟ أن المساجد لا تدخل في حيز ما يسمى بالكزرة، قد ذكرنا أن الكزرة هي الإحياء بالقسر أي التملك بقسر من غير إذن، والمساجد ملك عام للناس فليست ملكا شخصيا ومن هنا فلا تدخل في ذلك فهي لله سبحانه وتعالى حررها من ملك العباد ومن ملك الأغيار فلا تدخل في هذا القبيل أصلا.
body_en:
Question: Some of the imams last Friday say that prayer in this mosque is not valid, because it is makzūr [built on land taken by al-kazrah]?

Answer: Mosques do not fall within the scope of what is called al-kazrah. We have already mentioned that al-kazrah is bringing land into use by force — that is, taking ownership by force, without permission. Mosques are the common property of the people; they are not personal property. Hence they do not fall within that. They belong to God, glorified and exalted; He has freed them from the ownership of [His] servants and from the ownership of others, so they do not fall into this category at all.

flags.context: أن المساجد لا تدخل في حيز ما يسمى بالكزرة، قد ذكرنا أن الكزرة هي الإحياء بالقسر أي التملك بقسر من غير إذن
flags.note: "Al-kazrah" (also written الگزرة) is a Mauritanian dialect term for occupying and building on land without official allocation; the title’s "ghayr mushraʿ" ("not lawfully allocated/authorised") points the same way. The Sheikh supplies his own definition in the answer — "bringing land into use by force, that is, taking ownership by force without permission" — which has been translated rather than replaced by an English legal term, since "squatting" and "land-grabbing" carry connotations the Arabic may not. Note also that the Sheikh answers only that mosques fall outside the category; he does not state in so many words that the prayer is valid, and no such statement has been supplied.
